subject: Measure of central tendency for ordinal values

messages.author: 64dd3e60f9213f7d
messages.subject: Measure of central tendency for ordinal values
parts:
Dear all,

Suppose you have an ordinal variable (values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, etc.) and you want to visualize the distribution of the variable's levels using for example bar plots. The appropriate measure of central tendency for ordinal values seems to be the median (the middle value of the ordered values), while the means seems to be dispreferred (a means of, say, 3.57 for ordinal values constructs a value that does not, and cannot, exist). Suppose further that, for your data in hand, the median is of little use simply because all the variable's levels happen to have the same median and, hence, the bar plots for the medians would be the same too.

1. In that case, and providing you account for that case in your report, is the use of the means for visualization justifiable?

2. If using the means is totally unacceptable, even for simple visualization, is there another measure, beside the median, which does bring out more subtle differences and which is acceptable?

Thanks in advance

Best
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Measure of central tendency for ordinal values
parts: I'm no statistician, so take what I say with a grain of salt. Since median is the preferred measure of location here, I don't see why you wouldn't use it. However, since you say you want to visualize the variable's distribution, not its location, maybe you want a measure of spread like MAD (median absolute deviation)?

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Measure of central tendency for ordinal values
parts: > The appropriate measure of central tendency for ordinal values seems to be the median
Yes.
> while the means seems to be dispreferred (a means of, say, 3.57 for ordinal values constructs a value that does not, and cannot, exist).

That is in fact not really such a strong argument because the median
of c(1,2,3,4) is 2.5, which also does not and cannot exist.

> Suppose further that, for your data in hand, the median is of little use simply because all the variable's levels happen to have the same median and, hence, the bar plots for the medians would be the same too.

Well, but what does it mean, "of little use simply because all the
variable's levels happen to have the same median" - if that's the
empirical finding, what does "of little use" mean? If they all have
the same median (such that, e.g., a Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA says there
are no significant differences), then THAT is the finding and a bar
plot should represent exactly that, no?
> 1. In that case, and providing you account for that case in your report, is the use of the means for visualization justifiable?
I would not use it.
> 2. If using the means is totally unacceptable, even for simple visualization, is there another measure, beside the median, which does bring out more subtle differences and which is acceptable?

Why barplots of medians at all? Why not boxplots or, even more
precise, ecdf plots?

Cheers,
STG
